> **Design reference — implemented on real data.** This is the research grounding for
> [`ConveyVerb.kt`](../src/commonMain/kotlin/compose/conveyance/ConveyVerb.kt) and
> [`ConveyKineticSentence`](../src/commonMain/kotlin/compose/conveyance/ConveyKineticText.kt),
> which implement this report's architecture directly against **Princeton WordNet 3.0** (full
> ~11,500-verb-lemma index, all senses' domains and glosses, the real `verb.exc` irregular-form
> table) and **VerbNet 3.3** (all 325 top-level classes' member lists and `SEMANTICS`/`PRED`
> predicates), including a real Simplified Lesk word-sense-disambiguation pass
> (§"Deterministic Word Sense Disambiguation and Coercion Detection") scored against actual
> WordNet glosses. The compiled data lives in
> [`internal/ConveyVerbData.kt`](../src/commonMain/kotlin/compose/conveyance/internal/ConveyVerbData.kt)
> (generated — do not hand-edit; see **Generation pipeline** below to regenerate it).
>
> What is still **not** implemented, and why: Levin's classification is subsumed here by VerbNet
> (VerbNet is itself built on and extends Levin's classes, so there is no separate Levin layer to
> add). **FrameNet** (§"FrameNet: Conceptual Structures versus Syntactic Alternations") is not
> used at all — no FrameNet data was fetched or parsed. The report's own worked FrameNet example
> (grouping bake/boil/fry/roast/simmer under one `Apply_heat` frame) is reproduced here, but by
> coincidence of VerbNet's own class boundaries: VerbNet's `cooking-45.3` class happens to group
> exactly those verbs behind `apply_heat`/`cooked` predicates, so `StateMetaphor` gets the right
> answer for the right *example* without the right *mechanism* — a real FrameNet layer would need
> its own dataset this implementation doesn't have. The report's own Aktionsart grouping of
> "read, kill, find, build" as one Scalar class reflects a telic/atelic (Vendler) distinction that
> neither WordNet's domains nor VerbNet's predicates encode directly — `ConveyVerbClass.Scalar`
> here captures only the narrower VerbNet-supported subset (verbs of degree/value change, e.g.
> "soar"). The report's "Volume" loudness tier (shout vs. speak vs. whisper) has no signal in
> either resource used here, so it isn't a separate case — loud verbs classify as `Communication`
> like any other. **VerbNet's event-timeline / GL-VerbNet subevent modeling**
> (§"Event Timeline Modeling and Subevent Sequences via VerbNet", §"Generative Lexicon (GL-VerbNet)
> State Tracking") is not implemented either: this pipeline reads a VerbNet class's `PRED` values
> only as a flat *set*, to pick one static `ConveyVerbClass`, and never touches the report's
> tripartite preparatory/culmination/consequent event structure or GL-VerbNet's precondition/
> postcondition state changes — there is no keyframe-timeline layer here, only a single discrete
> classification per sense. And genuinely: VerbNet's own class judgments are sometimes broader
> than intuition expects (documented with a real example — "yell" — on `ConveyVerbClass`'s own
> doc comment), and Simplified Lesk can fail to disambiguate when a sentence's vocabulary doesn't
> literally overlap any candidate gloss, a known, inherent limitation of the algorithm itself, not
> of this implementation. Nor is **selectional-restriction-based syntactic coercion**
> (§"Selectional Restrictions and Syntactic Coercion") implemented — see
> `ConveyKineticSentence`'s own doc comment for why (no parser; every verb classifies from its own
> WordNet/VerbNet senses in isolation, never from its surrounding syntactic frame). Nor is the
> report's **static topographical/concrete-poetry layout**
> (§"Static Topographical Alignment and Concrete Poetry") **is** now implemented — generalized
> past the report's one worked example (a downward staircase for descent verbs) into an actual
> procedural generator:
> [`ConveyTopographicalLayout`](../src/commonMain/kotlin/compose/conveyance/foundation/ConveyTopographicalLayout.kt)
> picks its own shape from
> [`ConveyVerbLexicon.topographicalCategory`](../src/commonMain/kotlin/compose/conveyance/ConveyVerb.kt),
> which resolves a sentence's own verb to one of four categories (`Descent`, `Ascent`, `Scatter`,
> `Encircle`), each via a keyword check against that verb's real resolved WordNet gloss — not a
> hypernym chain: WordNet's own hypernym depth for near-synonyms like "fall" and "descend" is
> inconsistent enough that chain-ancestor traversal missed several of the report's own examples;
> gloss vocabulary catches them, since WordNet definitions themselves tend to cross-reference the
> same handful of words for the same concept. Each category drives its own
> [`ConveyTopographicalPath`](../src/commonMain/kotlin/compose/conveyance/foundation/ConveyTopographicalLayout.kt)
> — a one-function interface, so a fifth shape is a fifth function, not a fork of the layout
> engine. A sentence whose verb matches none of the four still renders — as ordinary flowing
> text, deliberately, rather than forcing a shape that doesn't fit.
>
> ## Generation pipeline
>
> `ConveyVerbData.kt` was produced by a Python pipeline (not checked into this repo) run against:
> - Princeton WordNet 3.0's `index.verb`, `data.verb`, and `verb.exc`
>   (`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nltk/nltk_data/gh-pages/packages/corpora/wordnet.zip`).
> - VerbNet 3.3's class XML corpus
>   (`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nltk/nltk_data/gh-pages/packages/corpora/verbnet3.zip`).
>
> Pipeline, in order: (1) parse `data.verb`/`index.verb` into synset offset → (domain, gloss) and
> lemma → sense-ordered offset list; parse `verb.exc` into inflected → base-form pairs. (2) parse
> every VerbNet class (recursing into `SUBCLASSES`) into its member list and the union of its
> frames' `SEMANTICS`/`PRED` values; resolve each `MEMBER`'s `wn="lemma%2:LL:II"` sense key(s) —
> a member can list more than one, and all are honored — to the exact WordNet synset offset they
> name. (3) classify each VerbNet class into a `ConveyVerbClass` refinement via a priority rule
> table: known Levin-chapter class-ID prefixes first (e.g. `cooking-45.3` → `StateMetaphor`,
> `run-51.3` → `MannerAgent`, `break-45.1` → `Punctual`), then predicate-based fallback rules
> (`degradation_material_integrity` → `Punctual`; `contact`+`exert_force` → `Contact`;
> `emotional_state` → `Emotion`; `perceive` → `Perception`). (4) emit one refinement per resolved
> WordNet offset (never per lemma — a verb's other senses are untouched) plus the full WordNet
> domain/gloss/lemma/exception tables, as a compact tab-delimited blob, chunked into ≤40,000-byte
> pieces (JVM's per-string-constant limit is 65,535 UTF-8 bytes) and emitted as Kotlin raw-string
> array literals.
>
> `ConveyVerbLexicon.classify` builds, per WordNet sense (in frequency order), a candidate class —
> the VerbNet-refined class for that exact sense if one was resolved, else the sense's coarse
> WordNet domain — and returns it directly when every sense agrees. On disagreement, with context,
> it runs Simplified Lesk (gloss/context word-overlap, excluding the query word's own inflected
> forms so a gloss's self-referential example sentence can't spuriously "win"); without a clear
> winner it falls back to the primary (most frequent) sense, deterministically.

# **Architecting a Deterministic, Context-Aware Kinetic Typography Engine Through Lexical Semantic Verb Classification**

## **Introduction**

The written word is one of humanity’s most powerful and enduring communicative inventions, yet its basic static presentation has remained largely unchanged for millennia1. The advent of digital rendering introduced kinetic typography—text that utilizes movement, morphology, or other temporal changes to convey emotion, portray compelling character archetypes, and visually direct audience attention1. By infusing typography with kinetic behaviors, designers can harness the expressive power of film and animation to augment the strong communicative properties of text1. Historically, the creation of kinetic text relied heavily on manual keyframe animation utilizing proprietary software such as Adobe After Effects, often requiring designers to hack or circumnavigate program constraints to manipulate detailed typographic properties5. While early computational research yielded programmatic precursors—such as WordsEye or CarSim, which utilized rule-based natural language processing to automatically generate 3D scenes or animations from text6—modern approaches increasingly default to opaque, computationally expensive machine learning models.  
To engineer a context-aware kinetic text engine exclusively through deterministic, rule-based logic—bypassing neural networks entirely—system architects must mathematically classify, categorize, and simplify all verbs in the English language. The verb is the structural and kinetic core of any sentence; it dictates argument realization, determines spatial and temporal relationships, and fundamentally encodes the physics of the described event. By establishing a rigorous taxonomy that maps the semantic and syntactic behaviors of verbs to physical animation parameters (such as force dynamics, spatial translation, and variable font interpolation), a rule-based engine can interpret natural language context and render fluid typographic motion. This report details the theoretical linguistic framework and applied programmatic methodology necessary to construct such an engine. It synthesizes foundational lexical resources, including Levin's Verb Classes, VerbNet, and WordNet, with classical animation principles and modern CSS variable font specifications. Through this exhaustive synthesis, the report provides a blueprint for translating the complex semantics of the English language into procedural, context-aware visual expression.

## **The Semantic Foundation: Categorizing Verbs in the English Language**

There is a vast and highly polysemous verb lexicon in the English language, with individual verbs frequently shifting meaning and argument structure depending on context7. Constructing a deterministic kinetic engine requires reducing this sprawling complexity into finite, machine-readable categories. The historical bedrock of computational verb classification relies on the inherent correlation between a verb's semantic meaning and its syntactic behavior.

### **Levin’s Verb Classes and Syntactic Alternations**

The foremost methodological tool for grouping verbs in the English language is the alternation test established by Beth Levin8. Levin’s core hypothesis dictates that the behavior of a verb, particularly regarding the expression and interpretation of its arguments, is predominantly determined by its meaning8. Verbs sharing specific semantic components tend to exhibit identical syntactic alternation patterns—systematic variations in how their argument structures are realized8. For example, diathesis alternations include the dative alternation (alternating between a prepositional frame and a double-object frame) and the benefactive alternation10. By executing these alternation tests, Levin mapped the semantic arguments to syntactic positions, creating a hierarchical taxonomy comprising approximately 200 main verb classes, 79 types of alternations, and roughly 3,100 verbs8.  
For a kinetic text engine, Levin’s taxonomy acts as the foundational filtering layer. Instead of programming bespoke animation physics for thousands of individual words, the engine only requires core animation parameters for the generalized semantic classes. For instance, verbs in the "Spray/Load" class share a distinct relationship with spatial locations and themes, allowing for a unified visual routine involving the distribution of a mass over a surface or within a container9. Similarly, verbs belonging to the "Hit" class (e.g., *beat*, *kick*, *hit*) undergo the conative alternation and inherently imply physical contact, which translates programmatically into sudden impact scaling or typographic vibration upon coordinate intersection10.  
Levin's classification also exposes the micro-differences among verbs with clustered meanings by isolating elements like semantic behavior and morpho-syntactic behavior11. The engine can utilize these properties to determine kinetic duration and resolution.

| Semantic Property | Definition | Kinetic Typographic Implementation | Example Verbs |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Scalar | Verbs denoting an action with a definitive endpoint or accomplishment. | Animations utilizing ease-out temporal functions that resolve into a static, final state on the canvas. | *read*, *kill*, *find*, *build* |
| Non-scalar | Verbs denoting ongoing states, activities, or psychological conditions without a kinetic climax. | Continuous, looping animations using sine-wave oscillations or breathing effects. | *love*, *trust*, *see* |
| Continuous | Verbs possessing the ability to occur progressively over an extended duration. | Smooth, linear velocity translation across the XY coordinate plane. | *walk*, *run*, *flow* \[cite: 8, 11\] |
| Punctual | Verbs denoting an action that occurs at a specific, instant point in time. | Sudden, high-velocity typographic shifts with zero interpolation time. | *arrive*, *shatter*, *snap* |

While highly effective, Levin's classification presents certain discrepancies in academic literature; some resources report 3,024 verbs across 193 classes, while others report coverage of 3,100 verbs or 192 classes10. Furthermore, Levin's framework occasionally splits verbs that are close in meaning due to strict alternation rules. For instance, Levin defines a separate class for "Butter Verbs" (verbs morphologically related to zero-related nominals, paraphrased as 'put X on/in something') distinct from "Spray/Load Verbs," despite their kinetic similarities12. To optimize engine efficiency, a developer might intentionally collapse these structurally fragmented classes into a single visual execution subroutine.

### **FrameNet: Conceptual Structures versus Syntactic Alternations**

To build a truly robust context-aware engine, it is necessary to contrast Levin’s syntax-driven classification with FrameNet, a project that groups words according to the conceptual structures or frames that underlie them, deriving combinatorial patterns inductively from corpus evidence. FrameNet demonstrates that verbs grouped together might be semantically similar but possess no shared alternations, meaning that verbs sharing a Levin alternation might be split into two different FrameNet semantic frames.  
Understanding this distinction allows the text engine to group verbs visually based on conceptual outcomes rather than strict syntax. For example, FrameNet groups verbs of heating and cooking (e.g., *bake*, *boil*, *fry*, *roast*, *simmer*) into a single "Apply\_heat" frame. In contrast, Levin splits these into distinct classes because a verb like *bake* undergoes the causative/inchoative and middle alternations, whereas other cooking verbs do not. For a visual rendering engine, the conceptual outcome of applying heat—perhaps visualized by an upward drift of the typography, an increase in letter-spacing to simulate thermal expansion, or a color shift toward the red spectrum—is universal across these verbs. Therefore, cross-referencing Levin's classes with FrameNet frames allows the engine to optimize its animation library by lumping semantically related verbs into shared rendering matrices.

### **High-Level Domain Categorization via WordNet**

For verbs that lack robust mechanical sequences or exist as highly abstract concepts, the engine must rely on WordNet to assign generalized kinetic profiles. WordNet is a lexical database containing an index file of alphabetized words and a data file of synsets (synonym rings) with pointers detailing linguistic relationships13. Crucially, WordNet organizes the English lexicon using lexicographer files, which correspond to syntactic categories and partition all verbs in the English language into 15 distinct semantic domains based on general meaning14.  
These 15 domains—which include verbs of communication, consumption, cognition, emotion, perception, and possession—serve as a critical fail-safe14. If a parsed verb cannot be mapped to a specific physical animation, the engine references its WordNet lexicographer file. Verbs in the "communication" domain (e.g., *speak*, *inform*, *declare*) can trigger a global kinetic rule that visually originates the text from a central coordinate mimicking an acoustic wave. Verbs classified within the "emotion" domain, which represent affective states, can bypass spatial movement entirely and instead trigger variable font weight interpolations or color-space transitions to denote internal psychological changes14. Because WordNet is structured strictly as a dictionary rather than an encyclopedia—excluding narrow domains, highly specialized common nouns, and proper nouns—it remains computationally lightweight and highly effective for broad programmatic fallback categorization20.

## **Event Timeline Modeling and Subevent Sequences via VerbNet**

While Levin’s classes and WordNet domains provide macroscopic organization, a kinetic text engine requires granular, machine-readable logic to execute precise visual transitions over time. VerbNet serves as the primary lexical resource for this task, significantly extending Levin’s taxonomy into a hierarchical structure encompassing 274 first-level classes and over 5,200 verb senses21. VerbNet defines detailed semantic information for each syntactic frame, expressed as a conjunction of boolean semantic predicates such as MOTION, CONTACT, CAUSE, TRANSFER\_INFO, and EXERT\_FORCE22.

### **Parsing Predicates into Keyframe Animation**

The utility of VerbNet in procedural animation lies in its integration of predicates with specific event variables (![][image1]), effectively mapping language directly onto an animation timeline22. The timeline is divided into a preparatory stage (![][image2]), a culmination stage (![][image3]), and a consequent stage (![][image4])13. This tripartite structure aligns flawlessly with the traditional principles of animation (anticipation, action, follow-through).  
Consider the VerbNet entry for the "Spray" class (e.g., *Jessica sprayed the wall*). The semantics are decomposed into sequential logic:

> 1. ![][image5]  
> 2. ![][image6]  
> 3. ![][image7]  
> 4. ![][image8]26.

A rule-based text engine translates these predicates into visual triggers. During the ![][image2] phase, the system confirms the Theme (the paint text) is not at the Destination (the wall text) coordinate. During the culmination phase, the Agent triggers the ![][image9] predicate, calculating a trajectory vector to move the Theme across the DOM. At the ![][image4] phase, the spatial coordinates lock together, confirming the successful transfer of location.

### **Generative Lexicon (GL-VerbNet) State Tracking**

Classic VerbNet representations occasionally suffered from deficiencies in explicitly detailing the sequential subevents and precise state changes across the timespan of an event25. The introduction of Generative Lexicon (GL) structures to VerbNet refined these representations, allowing systems to extract definitive preconditions and postconditions. By switching to first-order logic representations, GL-VerbNet tracks exact state changes across subevents (![][image10], ![][image11], ![][image12], ![][image13]).

| Event Stage | Classic VerbNet Predicate Logic for: I put the book on the table. | GL-VerbNet Sub-Event Logic for: I put the book on the table. |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Precondition | path\_rel(start(E), Theme, ? Initial\_location, ch\_of\_loc, prep) | has\_location(e1, Theme, ? Initial\_Location) |
| Action Initiation | cause(Agent, E) | do(e2, Agent) |
| Culmination (Motion) | motion(during(E), Theme) | motion(e3, Theme, ? Trajectory) cause(e2, e3) |
| State Change | path\_rel(during(E), Theme, Trajectory, ch\_of\_loc, prep) | ¬has\_location(e4, Theme, ? Initial\_location) |
| Postcondition | path\_rel(end(E), Theme, ? Destination, ch\_of\_loc, prep) | has\_location(e4, Theme, Destination) \[cite: \] |

The explicit boolean transition from has\_location at ![][image10] to ¬has\_location and the new has\_location at ![][image13] provides an irrefutable mathematical trigger for updating the absolute positioning (Top/Left CSS properties) of the typographic strings on the visual canvas.

### **Addressing Granularity in Motion Verbs**

While mapping path\_rel predicates yields accurate macroscopic translations, motion verbs contain deep internal semantic granularity that must be respected to avoid homogenous, lifeless animations8. To differentiate the verbs *stroll*, *stagger*, and *shiver*, the engine must reference the ten-level hierarchical classification of motion verbs8.  
This hierarchy separates motion into a literal layer and a metaphorical layer, exploring whether the verb encodes specific "path" information, depends on agent-specific physical properties, or shows subtle bodily movements8.

> 1. **Pure Path Verbs:** (e.g., *go*, *come*) Translated as constant-velocity linear translation without specific manner modifiers8.  
> 2. **Manner Verbs (Agent Properties):** (e.g., *limp*, *stagger*) Translated by applying asymmetric, arrhythmic vertical baseline shifts over the primary translation path, utilizing unequal temporal timing functions to simulate an uneven gait8.  
> 3. **Subtle Body Movements:** (e.g., *shiver*, *tremble*) Translated by applying high-frequency, low-amplitude positional vibrations to individual glyphs without altering the macro-path coordinate1.  
> 4. **State Metaphor:** (e.g., *soar*) Translated by applying an ease-out vertical upward trajectory paired with dynamic typographic lightening (reducing font weight), mapping spatial motion to an emotional or psychological uplift8.

## **Deterministic Word Sense Disambiguation and Coercion Detection**

The primary vulnerability of a deterministic natural language engine is polysemy—the capacity for a single verb to evoke entirely distinct semantics and syntactic frames depending on the surrounding text7. For example, the verb *serve* inhabits four separate Levin classes (Give, Fit, Masquerade, and Fulfilling), while *study* shifts between Learn, Sight, and Assessment depending on context10. If the engine misinterprets *write* as a Performance verb rather than a Message Transfer verb, the resulting typographic display will inherently fail to match the author's intent10.  
Because the system constraint explicitly prohibits stochastic machine learning, the engine must rely on deterministic, knowledge-source algorithms for Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD).

### **The Simplified Lesk Algorithm**

The most viable non-ML approach to resolving semantic ambiguity is the Simplified Lesk Algorithm28. The core theoretical premise of Lesk's algorithm posits that a word's correct sense within a given sentence can be isolated by locating the maximum semantic overlap between the dictionary glosses (definitions) of the target word and the glosses of the surrounding context words29.  
When the kinetic engine tokenizes a sentence containing a polysemous verb, it queries the WordNet index files for the target verb and the neighboring nouns13. The Simplified Lesk Algorithm then mathematically calculates the intersection of their glosses28. For example, if the engine processes the phrase "studied the stars through the telescope," it cross-references the definitions of *study*, *star*, and *telescope*. The overlapping terminology related to vision, lenses, and astronomy definitively aligns the verb *study* with its "Sight" VerbNet class, immediately isolating the correct rendering matrix10. Recent computational advancements have introduced Bee Colony optimization and simulated annealing to the Simplified Lesk approach, dramatically improving the speed and accuracy of the context window search without requiring opaque neural networks28.

### **Selectional Restrictions and Syntactic Coercion**

An engine's WSD capability is further fortified by enforcing the explicit selectional restrictions encoded within VerbNet thematic roles23. VerbNet dictates precise semantic boundaries; an Agent may require \[+int\_control\] (intentional control), while a Patient may require \[+concrete\] properties.  
Monitoring these restrictions allows the system to deterministically isolate figurative language. The verb *destroy* (DESTROY-44 class) strictly demands a \[+concrete\] Patient. If the engine parses "The bomb destroyed the building," the \[+concrete\] restriction is satisfied, and a physical fragmentation or explosion animation is triggered. However, if the engine parses "The speaker destroyed his argument," the object (*argument*) evaluates as \[-concrete\]. This registered violation acts as a programmable logic fork, instructing the engine to abandon literal physics and substitute a metaphorical visual effect—such as reducing text opacity or applying an aggressive strike-through.  
Furthermore, syntactic frames can forcibly coerce non-motion verbs into kinetic paradigms through caused-motion constructions (CMC)24. Consider the sentence: "The crowd laughed the clown off the stage"32. The verb *laugh* is fundamentally a verb of non-verbal communication and lacks inherent motion entailments. However, a rule-based parser identifying the specific NP V NP PP syntax—where the prepositional phrase dictates a spatial trajectory—will override the verb's inherent static semantics5. The CMC pattern licenses the direct object and injects a new CAUSE and MOTION predicate into the sequence, coercing the engine to animate the subject (crowd) exerting a kinetic force that propels the object (clown) along a spatial path21.

## **The Taxonomy and Physics of Kinetic Typography**

Once the verb is classified, its sense disambiguated, and its subevent timeline extracted, the engine must translate this abstract computational logic into visual motion. Kinetic typography transforms text from a static plane into an immersive, temporal space4. Johnny C. Lee’s foundational Kinetic Typography Engine introduced a comprehensive taxonomy that categorizes text manipulation into structural adaptations of traditional animation and psychological representations of analogous motion1.

### **Global Kineticism, Local Kineticism, and Fluid Typography**

To programmatically execute VerbNet logic, the engine divides text behavior into two distinct categories: global and local kineticism.  
Global kineticism involves changes of location that affect the overall layout of the text, such as scrolling, tracking, or path-following across the screen. Verbs possessing path\_rel or explicit MOTION predicates mapped to trajectories inherently trigger global kinetic routines23. Conversely, local kineticism affects the specific morphological appearance and identity of individual letterforms without translating their macro-position on the canvas. Local kineticism is instrumental in rendering fluid typography—where letterforms abandon one identity and adopt another to reflect internal state changes. Verbs denoting internal psychological shifts, or those categorized by WordNet’s "emotion" domain, primarily trigger local kinetic routines.

### **Analogous Motion and Force Dynamics**

The most powerful communicative aspect of kinetic typography is its ability to mimic human actions to convey complex affective content1. The rule-based engine must map semantic verb traits to these established analogous motions:

* **High Arousal/High Energy:** Verbs denoting anger, excitement, or anticipation trigger small, rapid, high-frequency vibrations analogous to human trembling.  
* **Low Arousal/Negative Valence:** Verbs denoting disappointment or sadness trigger slow, shrinking motions analogous to slumping shoulders.  
* **Empathy/Calm:** Verbs describing peaceful states trigger slow, rhythmic expansions and contractions reminiscent of calm breathing.  
* **Volume and Tone:** Verbs of shouting trigger massive scale expansions accompanied by shake effects to simulate reverberation, while diminutive verbs stick rigidly to the baseline with slow pacing.

For sentences involving multiple entities (Agent and Patient), the engine governs interaction through explicit force dynamics35. Empirical studies demonstrate that humans naturally interpret social interactions through the compositional nature of physical forces35. By calculating vector combinations, the engine applies interactive forces—driven by verbs containing CONTACT or CAUSE predicates (yielding magnetic attraction or violent repulsion)—and self-propelled forces—driven by verbs of independent motion generating autonomous kinetic energy. In experimental tasks, mathematical models representing these compositional forces achieved high correlation (r \= 0.520) with human judgments of social interaction, proving that deterministic force parameters can accurately simulate complex social dynamics on a typographic canvas.

### **Static Topographical Alignment and Concrete Poetry**

While temporal animation provides dynamic expression, the engine can also execute non-animated text rearrangements to be displayed statically, a practice rooted in the tradition of concrete (or visual/shape) poetry38. In concrete poetry, the visual appearance, typographical layout, and fixed arrangement of linguistic elements are as critical as the literal text, often forming a shape that visually elucidates the subject38. A famous historical example is Lewis Carroll's 1865 calligram, "The Mouse's Tale," where the words are arranged in a long, winding shape to mimic a literal mouse's tail, compounding the narrative's meaning purely through its static layout39.  
To implement this algorithmically without an active animation timeline, the engine maps a verb's semantic path directly into static coordinate geometry42. For example, if the engine parses a verb denoting a cascading downward movement or descent (such as *fall*, *descend*, or *step down*), it can trigger a static typographical alignment rule. Instead of moving the text over time via keyframes, the algorithm calculates a static DOM layout where each successive word is rendered on a new line, incrementally shifting the horizontal offset (X-coordinate or tab spacing) rightward just beyond the end of the preceding word. This constraint-based procedural layout constructs a visual staircase, allowing the sentence itself to physically and statically manifest the physics of the verb through its topographical alignment38.

## **Architectural Blueprint for Jetpack Compose**

To implement this rule-based engine for modern mobile or desktop applications, Jetpack Compose provides an ideal declarative UI framework. Unlike the legacy XML TextView system in Android—which relies on an imperative onDraw() cycle that is computationally expensive to continuously invalidate and re-measure—Compose utilizes a Skia-based rendering engine43. By leveraging the TextMeasurer, Compose handles text shaping and GPU-accelerated rasterization directly, making it highly performant for dynamic kinetic text3.

### **Conceptual Algorithm**

The engine's pipeline in Compose follows a deterministic sequence:

> 1. **Lexical Parsing:** Tokenize the input string and run the Simplified Lesk Algorithm to disambiguate the verb sense.  
> 2. **Sequence Extraction:** Retrieve the GL-VerbNet first-order logic predicates for the disambiguated verb.  
> 3. **Physics Mapping:** Map the boolean state changes to continuous numerical states (e.g., mapping a MOTION predicate to a spatial vector, or an emotion domain to a font weight multiplier).  
> 4. **Compose State Driven Animation:** Feed these parameters into Jetpack Compose reactive State\<Float\> variables, driven by animateFloatAsState or specific keyframe animation specs.

Within Compose, local kineticism (fluid typography) is achieved natively using OpenType variable fonts via the FontVariation.Settings API44. Standard axes can be accessed via helper functions like FontVariation.weight() and FontVariation.width(), while custom axes use FontVariation.Setting("TAG", value)45.  
A conceptual Compose mapping for a sudden, aggressive verb sequence might look like this:

Kotlin  
// Example conceptual Compose mapping for an impactful verb  
val animatedWeight by animateFloatAsState(  
    targetValue \= if (isActionActive) 900f else 400f,  
    animationSpec \= tween(durationMillis \= 300, easing \= FastOutSlowInEasing)  
)

Text(  
    text \= "SHATTER",  
    fontFamily \= FontFamily(  
        Font(  
            R.font.variable\_type,  
            variationSettings \= FontVariation.Settings(  
                FontVariation.weight(animatedWeight)  
            )  
        )  
    )  
)

Because Compose drives the font axis values directly as reactive state, the text redraws smoothly at high framerates without the massive layout overhead of traditional UI toolkits43.

### **Evaluation: Native (C++/Rust) vs. Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP)**

When architecting the core logic of this engine (the NLP parser, the VerbNet lookup, and the physics vector calculators), developers must decide between a Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) approach and a pure Native (C++ or Rust) approach.  
KMP offers significant architectural benefits by allowing the complex linguistic business logic to be written once in Kotlin and shared across Android, iOS, and Desktop, while seamlessly interfacing with native UI toolkits like Jetpack Compose46. For most general applications, KMP provides excellent, near-native performance5.  
However, for a heavily computational kinetic engine that needs to calculate physics vectors for thousands of text particles simultaneously, a pure Native core (written in Rust or C++) bound to the UI via a Foreign Function Interface (FFI) offers definitive performance advantages47. Kotlin/Native relies on garbage collection (GC) which can occasionally trigger stop-the-world pauses (averaging 3–5ms) that drop frame rates during heavy memory allocations48. In benchmark testing against intensive algorithmic tasks (like matrix multiplication), Native implementations—such as WebAssembly or Rust backends—achieve up to 14% faster computation times and significantly lower peak memory usage due to deterministic memory lifetimes, entirely avoiding KMP's GC overhead.  
Therefore, while KMP is sufficient for basic typography manipulation and offers rapid multiplatform adoption, a true physics-driven text engine aiming for a locked 60+ FPS across thousands of glyphs would ultimately perform best with a Rust or C++ core that calculates the states and feeds the numerical data directly to the Compose UI layer.

## **Conclusion**

The theoretical construction of a context-aware kinetic text engine, devoid of stochastic machine learning models, represents a masterclass in the synthesis of computational linguistics and modern rendering architectures. By systematically parsing the English lexicon through Levin’s syntactic alternations, engines can group sprawling verb behaviors into manageable, programmable classes. This macroscopic categorization is refined by VerbNet’s first-order logical predicates, which extract explicit event timelines and state-change parameters, effectively writing the choreography for typographic motion. By employing the Simplified Lesk Algorithm for precise word sense disambiguation, and enforcing selectional restrictions to identify figurative coercion, the system guarantees accurate contextual awareness.  
Finally, the engine bridges the gap between semantic theory and visual execution by applying Johnny C. Lee's taxonomy of kinetic motion to the mathematical capabilities of OpenType variable fonts. By mapping specific physical and emotional traits to continuous design axes, and rendering them through modern declarative frameworks like Jetpack Compose, static text is transformed into a highly performant, responsive visual medium. This architecture proves that the exhaustive categorization of all verbs in the English language is not merely an academic exercise, but the definitive algorithmic blueprint for breathing autonomous, deterministic life into the written word.
